issues.note: Covers articles indexed since yesterday's run. No big ED drug RCTs this window, so most picks are cohorts and trial secondary analyses; read the observational items as hypothesis-generating.
bottom_line: Patients discharged after stimulant toxicity have meaningful 1-year mortality, mostly from opioid-involved overdose. Offer naloxone at discharge even when the visit was for meth or cocaine.
Nebulized TXA for stable post-tonsillectomy bleeding with a small clot sharply cut the need for surgery in kids. It's a cheap, low-risk ED option worth a protocol.
Intra-arterial tenecteplase after thrombectomy helped mainly when reperfusion was incomplete (eTICI 2b50–67), not after near-complete reperfusion.

articles.takeaway: About 2% of patients died within a year of an ED visit for stimulant toxicity, mostly from opioid-involved overdoses
articles.title: One-year mortality following emergency department visits for stimulant toxicity.
articles.population: 2,356 patients discharged from the ED with stimulant toxicity, US statewide linked database
articles.summary: Linked ED, hospital and death records showed 1-year all-cause mortality of 2.1% after ED discharge for stimulant toxicity. Those who died were young (median age 35) and died a median of 118 days after the visit. Two-thirds of deaths were overdoses, and opioids were involved in 54% of them. A reference cohort of opioid-toxicity visits had higher 1-year mortality (6.9%).
articles.why: Supports giving naloxone and harm-reduction counseling to stimulant patients at ED discharge, since the fentanyl supply drives much of their later risk.

articles.takeaway: In witnessed pediatric OHCA, earlier epinephrine wasn't clearly linked to better 1-month survival
articles.title: Timing of the Adrenaline Administration in Witnessed Pediatric Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: Retrospective, National Cohort Study in Japan, Using a 2014-2020 Dataset.
articles.population: 259 children with witnessed OHCA who received epinephrine, Japanese national registry (JAAM-OHCA)
articles.summary: The authors used time-dependent propensity score risk-set matching to reduce resuscitation time bias, comparing children given epinephrine in each time window with children not yet given it. None of the time windows (1–10 up to 26–30 minutes after EMS contact) showed a significant difference in 1-month survival or favorable neurologic outcome. Confidence intervals were very wide (e.g., RR 2.94, 95% CI 0.38–22.8 for 1–10 minutes), so the study was underpowered to detect a real effect.
articles.why: A null result from a small sample doesn't overturn the push for early epinephrine in pediatric arrest. Keep weight-based doses ready, and read this as a lack of power rather than proof of no benefit.

articles.takeaway: Adjunctive cenobamate ended most refractory focal status epilepticus cases in a real-world cohort
articles.title: Cenobamate in Focal-Onset Refractory and Super-Refractory Status Epilepticus: A Multicenter Cohort Study With Matched Analysis.
articles.population: 31 adults with focal refractory or super-refractory SE, multicenter registry (Spain), plus 56 matched controls
articles.summary: Cenobamate was started a median of 4 days into SE, after 5 failed antiseizure meds, at a median of 50 mg/day enterally. SE resolved in 84% (all RSE patients and 64% of SRSE), with response at a median of 2 days. In the propensity-matched comparison, resolution was more common with cenobamate (82% vs 57%; aOR 5.9). No serious drug-related adverse events occurred, and somnolence was the most common mild effect.
articles.why: Cenobamate is enteral-only and slow to titrate, so it's a late ICU add-on rather than an ED option. Watch for its interactions (it raises phenytoin and phenobarbital levels and lowers lamotrigine levels).

articles.takeaway: Intra-arterial tenecteplase after thrombectomy helped only when reperfusion was incomplete
articles.title: Relationship Between the eTICI Score Before Randomization and 90-Day Outcome: A Post Hoc Analysis of ANGEL-TNK Trial.
articles.population: 253 patients with anterior-circulation LVO after successful EVT, multicenter China (ANGEL-TNK)
articles.summary: Patients were randomized to intra-arterial tenecteplase 0.125 mg/kg or standard care after eTICI 2b50 or better reperfusion. With partial reperfusion (eTICI 2b50–67), tenecteplase more than doubled the rate of mRS 0–1 at 90 days (44.8% vs 19.5%; RR 2.08). With near-complete reperfusion (eTICI 2c–3), it gave no benefit and raised any ICH within 48 hours (33.3% vs 20.0%), though symptomatic ICH and death didn't differ.
articles.why: Helps answer which post-EVT patients should get IA lytic. Expect neuro-IR to ask about TNK dosing for patients with residual distal occlusion.

articles.takeaway: IV N-acetylcysteine was linked to lower 21-day mortality in acute liver failure not caused by acetaminophen
articles.title: Evaluation of the Association of N-Acetylcysteine and Mortality in Non-Acetaminophen-Induced Acute Liver Failure.
articles.population: 200 adults with non-acetaminophen acute liver failure (85 got IV NAC), single US center
articles.summary: After inverse probability weighting for severity, comorbidities and etiology, IV NAC was associated with lower in-hospital mortality at 21 days (48.9% vs 62.1%; OR 0.59). Time to INR and LFT normalization and length of stay didn't differ. The study is retrospective and single-center, so unmeasured confounding remains possible.
articles.why: Supports starting the IV NAC protocol early in non-APAP ALF, for example from drugs, herbals or mushrooms, while transplant is being considered. Its low risk favors giving it when the etiology is unclear.

articles.takeaway: Nebulized TXA cut surgery for pediatric post-tonsillectomy bleeding, especially with small clots
articles.title: Nebulized Tranexamic Acid in Posttonsillectomy Hemorrhage: A Retrospective Study of a Standardized Treatment Algorithm.
articles.population: 121 children presenting to the ED with post-tonsillectomy hemorrhage, 1 US tertiary children's hospital
articles.summary: Starting in March 2024, stable children got nebulized TXA and were then triaged by clot size. Overall surgery rates were 66% with TXA vs 80% before the protocol (not significant). Among children with small clots (under 50% of the fossa), surgery dropped from 88% to 21%. No TXA adverse events were reported, and the authors estimated 32 surgeries avoided and about $138,000 saved.
articles.why: An easy order set item for the ED, usually the IV TXA solution given by nebulizer. Pharmacists can standardize the dose and concentration.

articles.takeaway: After DAPT, clopidogrel beat aspirin monotherapy in higher-risk PCI patients without more bleeding
articles.title: Clopidogrel Versus Aspirin Monotherapy According to Atherothrombotic Risk Profile.
articles.population: 5,506 post-PCI patients after completing DAPT, SMART-CHOICE 3 trial (South Korea)
articles.summary: Patients were grouped by TIMI secondary-prevention risk score and PCI complexity. In the higher-risk group (82% of patients), clopidogrel reduced death, MI or stroke compared with aspirin (4.6% vs 7.4%; HR 0.67) over a median of 2.3 years. Lower-risk patients showed no difference, and the interaction test wasn't significant. Bleeding was similar across groups.
articles.why: Adds weight to clopidogrel as long-term single antiplatelet therapy after PCI. Remember CYP2C19 poor metabolizers and the PPI interaction (avoid omeprazole and esomeprazole).

articles.takeaway: A third of children delabeled from penicillin allergy still never received penicillin again
articles.title: Beyond delabeling: long-term penicillin use and avoidance following negative penicillin challenge in children.
articles.population: 305 children referred for penicillin allergy evaluation, 1 Israeli pediatric allergy clinic
articles.summary: Most children had a direct oral challenge (94%), and 98.6% tolerated it. Full tolerance, including a 5-day home course, was confirmed in 80%. Among tolerant children with follow-up, 64% later used penicillin again with no reactions, while 36% had no documented use. Younger age and less time since the challenge predicted reuse.
articles.why: Delabeling only works if the EHR allergy entry is actually removed. ED pharmacists can check for a negative challenge and remove stale labels before defaulting to broader agents.

issues.note: Off-schedule Thursday run covering everything added since Wednesday's issue. No major EM drug RCTs landed, so most picks are cohorts and reviews; read the observational items as hypothesis-generating.
bottom_line: For ED headache, start with a dopamine antagonist rather than an opioid. Opioid-first patients returned to the ED more often within 72 hours.
Concentrated 7-OH kratom tablets can deliver many times the opioid dose of leaf kratom and caused a fatal opioid toxidrome. Treat these exposures as opioid overdoses.
Protect multi-dose ketamine vials from light. A nitrosamine impurity built up past the acceptable limit in clear vials after light exposure.

articles.takeaway: Opioid-first ED headache treatment was linked to more 72-hour returns than dopamine antagonists
articles.title: Opioids as the earliest acute treatment for emergency department headache and short-term all-cause emergency department return: A two-center comparative cohort study.
articles.population: 13,285 adults treated for headache at 2 US academic EDs (MIMIC-IV-ED, MC-MED)
articles.summary: The study compared first-line opioids with guideline-preferred dopamine-receptor antagonists (e.g., prochlorperazine, metoclopramide). Among discharged patients, opioid-first treatment was associated with more all-cause ED returns at 72 hours (6.8% vs 3.8%; RR 1.78) and at 7 days (RR 1.62). The opioid group was older and higher acuity, and the signal weakened and lost significance when only headache-coded returns were counted.
articles.why: Adds real-world support for making dopamine antagonists the default on ED headache order sets. It's a useful data point when a prescriber reaches for hydromorphone first.

articles.takeaway: A concentrated 7-OH kratom tablet product caused a fatal opioid-like toxidrome
articles.title: Fatal Opioid-Like Toxidrome Associated With a 7-Hydroxymitragynine Kratom Product.
articles.population: 1 adult death after 3 commercial 7-HMG tablets plus alcohol, Louisiana
articles.summary: A 42-year-old man died after taking 3 tablets of a commercial 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-HMG) product with several beers. Autopsy showed severe pulmonary edema and a distended bladder, consistent with opioid toxicity. Each tablet held about 29 mg of 7-HMG plus mitragynine pseudoindoxyl, an even more potent μ-agonist. The total dose was roughly 19 to 87 times the 7-HMG exposure from a high dose of leaf kratom.
articles.why: Gas-station 7-OH products act like potent opioids. Expect respiratory depression, give naloxone, and ask specifically about these products when taking a med history.

articles.takeaway: Scheduling bromazolam lowered its presence in street opioids, but analogues replaced it
articles.title: Impact of drug scheduling on detection of bromazolam in the unregulated opioid supply: An interrupted time series analysis.
articles.population: 43,760 drug-checking samples, 142 sites in British Columbia, 2022–2026
articles.summary: Bromazolam detection in expected-opioid samples began falling after the WHO recommended scheduling it. It briefly jumped when China banned it, then settled below pre-scheduling levels. As bromazolam declined, another designer benzodiazepine (desalkylgidazepam) rose in its place. The authors conclude that scheduling broke the market into more substances rather than removing benzodiazepine adulteration.
articles.why: Benzo-adulterated opioid overdoses will keep producing sedation that lingers after naloxone. Standard urine benzo immunoassays may miss the newer designer analogues.

articles.takeaway: In HSCT neutropenic fever, time to antibiotics wasn't linked to deterioration
articles.title: Association between time-to-antibiotics and clinical outcomes in neutropenic fever after hematopoietic stem cell transplant.
articles.population: 224 antibiotic-naïve neutropenic fever episodes within 30 days of HSCT, 1 US academic center
articles.summary: Median time to antibiotics was 1.2 hours, and 38% of episodes got antibiotics within 1 hour. Getting antibiotics within an hour was not associated with clinical deterioration (vasopressors, ventilation, or 90-day death; aOR 1.18), and neither was each additional hour of delay (aOR 1.03). Only 17 patients deteriorated, so the study can't rule out a small effect.
articles.why: Challenges whether the 1-hour rule from septic shock applies to stable neutropenic fever. Treat it as hypothesis-generating; it isn't a reason to slow down cefepime or pip-tazo in the ED.

articles.takeaway: Prehospital opioids, ketamine, methoxyflurane and acetaminophen all look safe and effective for trauma pain
articles.title: Prehospital Analgesia in Trauma: A Systematic Review of Current Evidence.
articles.population: 17 studies (6 RCTs), 17,115 injured adults
articles.summary: The review covered studies from 2014 to 2026 of systemic prehospital analgesics in adult trauma patients. All agents relieved pain to some degree. Serious drug-related adverse events were reported in only one opioid study, while nausea, dizziness, dysphoria and drowsiness were common. Protocols and methods varied widely, which limits head-to-head conclusions.
articles.why: Supports giving analgesia early, before ED arrival. It's a reasonable reference when EMS and ED protocols are being aligned on ketamine and opioid dosing.

articles.takeaway: Light exposure of clear multi-dose ketamine vials drove nitrosamine levels above safety limits
articles.title: The photostability of ketamine products: part ii impact of light exposure and storage on multi-use ketamine parenteral products.
articles.population: 10 mg/mL multi-use ketamine vials under ambient and intense light, then stored
articles.summary: Researchers measured N-nitroso-ketamine (NNKet), a potentially carcinogenic nitrosamine impurity, in vials exposed to light and then stored. Levels dipped during light exposure and then rose sharply in storage, from about 5 ng/mL to as high as 100 ng/mL within 8 weeks. That is well above the 14 ng/mL acceptable-intake limit. Light-protected control vials barely changed.
articles.why: Store opened multi-dose ketamine vials protected from light (in cartons or ADC pockets) and follow beyond-use dates. Expect future packaging or labeling changes, such as amber vials.

articles.takeaway: In AF patients 80 and older, continuing anticoagulation was linked to lower mortality
articles.title: Anticoagulation and All-Cause Mortality in Adults Aged 80 Years and Older with Atrial Fibrillation: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
articles.population: 45,305 adults aged ≥80 with AF, large US health system
articles.summary: In a time-varying Cox model, anticoagulation was associated with 25% lower all-cause mortality (HR 0.75). One-year mortality was 8.7% in patients who continued anticoagulation and 17.7% in those never treated. GI bleeding was more common with anticoagulation, but intracranial hemorrhage rates were low and similar across groups (1.3–1.6%). The mortality difference faded by 5 years, and residual confounding is likely.
articles.why: Age alone shouldn't stop a DOAC. This study is a counterweight to Wednesday's nursing-home discontinuation data, so look at frailty and goals of care, not birth year.

articles.takeaway: Low-dose esketamine around thoracic surgery cut chronic pain at 3 months
articles.title: Effects of perioperative esketamine infusion on chronic pain after video-assisted thoracoscopic lung resection: a multicentre, randomised, double-blind clinical trial.
articles.population: 914 adults undergoing VATS lung resection, multicenter China
articles.summary: Patients got esketamine (0.1 mg/kg bolus, 0.1 mg/kg/h intraoperatively, then 0.015 mg/kg/h for 48 hours) or saline. Chronic pain at 3 months was less common with esketamine (14.7% vs 21.2%; aOR 0.62). Early pain scores and rescue analgesic use were also lower, with no increase in adverse effects.
articles.why: Adds RCT support for sub-dissociative ketamine as an opioid-sparing adjunct. Racemic ketamine is roughly twice the esketamine dose, so convert carefully before applying these regimens.

issues.note: A light two-day window with no major EM pharmacotherapy RCTs, so most picks are meta-analyses, cohorts and reviews. Treat the observational items as hypothesis-generating.
bottom_line: Intranasal or buccal midazolam stops pediatric seizures about as well as IV benzos, works faster than rectal diazepam, and cuts early recurrence.
In warfarin-associated ICH, base 4F-PCC decisions on bleed severity and neuro status (GCS), not an INR cutoff alone.
Calcium shifts on trauma arrival go both ways, and some hypercalcemia followed empiric prehospital calcium. Check an ionized Ca before repeat dosing.

articles.takeaway: Intranasal/buccal midazolam matches IV benzos for pediatric seizures and gets in faster
articles.title: Efficacy and safety of intranasal and buccal midazolam versus intravenous, intramuscular, and rectal benzodiazepines for the termination of acute seizures in children: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.population: 23 RCTs, 2,238 children with acute seizures
articles.summary: Pooled RCTs found that transmucosal midazolam stopped seizures within 10 minutes at a rate similar to all comparators (RR 1.04) and better than rectal diazepam (RR 1.18). It also cut recurrence within 60 minutes (RR 0.62) and was given faster, shortening overall time to seizure control. Respiratory depression and hypoxia did not differ from the other routes.
articles.why: Supports IN/buccal midazolam as first-line rescue when there's no IV access. Worth knowing the dosing and the atomizer setup for peds codes and EMS handoffs.

articles.takeaway: In geriatric warfarin ICH, GCS predicted death and INR didn't; don't gate 4F-PCC on INR alone
articles.title: Is the International Normalized Ratio (INR) Enough? Reevaluating INR-Based Decision-Making for Four-Factor Prothrombin Complex Concentrate in Geriatric Warfarin-Associated Intracranial Hemorrhage: A Multicenter Cohort Study.
articles.population: 60 patients aged ≥65 with non-traumatic warfarin ICH, 5 Turkish centers
articles.summary: Patients who got 4F-PCC had higher INRs than those managed without it, but neither INR nor 4F-PCC use was independently linked to in-hospital mortality. Admission GCS was strongly protective (aOR 0.37 per point). The sample is small and the comparator group was mixed (vitamin K, FFP, or nothing), so the findings are hypothesis-generating.
articles.why: Supports current guidance that reversal follows bleed severity, not an INR threshold. That matters when an order is held waiting for a lab value.

articles.takeaway: About 1 in 4 trauma activations arrive with abnormal calcium, and some hypercalcemia followed prehospital calcium
articles.title: Prehospital factors associated with calcium derangements upon arrival to the trauma center from scene - A subanalysis of a multicenter prospective study.
articles.population: 1,047 highest-level trauma activations arriving by EMS, 3 US trauma centers
articles.summary: On arrival, 235 patients were hypocalcemic and 39 were hypercalcemic, and both groups survived less often than patients with normal calcium. Hypocalcemia showed up even in patients who got no blood or fluids (16%), and 5 of the 39 hypercalcemic patients had received prehospital calcium. High shock index was associated with both problems, but nothing in the prehospital assessment reliably predicted which way calcium would go.
articles.why: Argues for checking ionized Ca on arrival over reflexive repeat calcium dosing. Relevant to MTP order sets and protocols for empiric calcium with blood products.

articles.takeaway: SubQ insulin pathways for mild–moderate DKA look comparable to IV drips and may cut ICU use
articles.title: Subcutaneous insulin for mild-to-moderate diabetic ketoacidosis: a scoping review and implementation framework.
articles.population: 13 adult studies of SUBQ insulin for DKA
articles.summary: Across 13 mostly small, single-center studies, subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin protocols reached DKA resolution in about the same time as IV insulin in selected patients with uncomplicated DKA. They also showed operational gains in ICU admissions and ED length of stay. The authors propose a framework for patient selection, dosing and monitoring, and note that higher-risk groups were excluded from most studies.
articles.why: A pharmacist-friendly framework if your ED is building a SubQ DKA pathway. Check eligibility criteria and how glucose and potassium are monitored.

articles.takeaway: Adjunctive intra-arterial thrombolysis after thrombectomy improves mRS 0–1; the mortality signal is unresolved
articles.title: Functional Benefit and Safety of Adjunctive Intra-Arterial Thrombolysis After Successful Endovascular Thrombectomy: An Updated and Cumulative Meta-Analysis of Randomized Trials.
articles.population: 9 RCTs, 2,828 patients with LVO stroke after successful EVT
articles.summary: Intra-arterial alteplase, tenecteplase or urokinase given after successful reperfusion raised the chance of an excellent outcome (mRS 0–1; RR 1.27, I² 0%), and the effect held up in fragility testing. Overall 90-day mortality did not differ significantly (RR 1.04), but the estimate shifted toward harm after CHOICE-2 was added, and the authors say neutrality on survival can't be assumed.
articles.why: As post-EVT IA lytics spread, pharmacists may get asked about dosing and stocking. The benefit looks real, but the safety question is still open.

articles.takeaway: Global CO and pesticide poisoning burden has fallen sharply since 1990, but low-income regions lag
articles.title: Global, regional, and national burden of unintentional poisoning, 1990-2023: results from the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023.
articles.population: 204 countries and territories, 1990–2023
articles.summary: In 2023, unintentional poisoning by carbon monoxide and other (mostly pesticide) agents caused about 2.5 million cases and 69,805 deaths worldwide. Age-standardized DALY rates fell 47.5% since 1990, with a 58% drop for CO. Case fatality was highest in low-SDI regions. Drug and illicit-substance poisonings are not counted in this GBD category.
articles.why: Useful epidemiologic context for CO and organophosphate tox. Remember that it leaves out pharmaceutical and illicit-drug overdoses.

articles.takeaway: Stopping anticoagulation at nursing-home entry wasn't linked to more strokes in AF
articles.title: Stroke and Bleeding Risk in Long-Term Care Residents With Atrial Fibrillation Who Discontinue Anticoagulation.
articles.population: 15,426 Medicare LTC residents with AF on anticoagulation (mean age 83)
articles.summary: Using a target trial emulation with clone-censor weighting, residents who stopped anticoagulation had stroke risk (sHR 1.07) and bleeding risk (sHR 1.02) similar to those who continued. Mortality was higher in the group that stopped (HR 1.27), which probably reflects confounding by frailty and goals of care. Very high competing mortality and claims-based outcomes limit what the study can show.
articles.why: Useful for deprescribing talks in frail older adults. In the ED, expect more LTC patients with AF who are off anticoagulation.

articles.takeaway: Drug use–associated endocarditis is falling overall, but stimulant-linked cases are rising
articles.title: Changing National and Regional Trends in Drug Use-Associated Infective Endocarditis From 2016 to 2022.
articles.population: ~118,000 US DUA-IE hospitalizations, 2016–2022
articles.summary: National DUA-IE hospitalizations peaked in 2020 (about 18,700) and fell through 2022. Over the study period, the opioid-only share dropped from 49% to 40%, while opioid-plus-stimulant co-use rose from 23% to 29% and stimulant-only cases from 15% to 18%. The probability of stimulant involvement was highest in the Pacific division (0.59).
articles.why: Shapes empiric IE workups and harm-reduction counseling at ED discharge. MOUD alone won't address stimulant-driven injection risk.
